results.point_context:
### The recruiter between speed and questions

I open the screening system after a flood of applications. It helps me move people toward the right jobs, but it does not remove my responsibility. I may need to prepare an audit summary when a candidate asks whether the process was fair. I also face a hard question: when an applicant uses AI to write a résumé, is that a useful skill or too little effort? I use these tools daily, but I do not set policy. I keep the process moving while answering questions.

results.point_context:
### The business owner watching the clock

Each week, I check a dashboard for hiring time and cost. If we cannot fill roles fast enough, I feel that pressure as my decision. AI looks attractive: a hotel chain reported cutting hiring time from weeks to days, while another company reported lower hiring costs. But I also see the other side. If an AI tool is accused of discrimination, my name will be tied to the choice. I am carrying the risk of keeping the company running.

results.point_context:
## Why They See the Same Tool Differently

All three want the right person in the right job. But the stakes split: the applicant may lose a chance unseen; the recruiter must keep speed and explain the process; the owner must keep the company running and answer for the choice. Power is unequal: the applicant is judged, the recruiter runs a tool without choosing it, and the owner chooses it and carries the result. In New York City, yearly bias checks and public notice make speed not just a private choice: the recruiter must document the tool, and applicants must be told. One company stopped a tool after it rated women’s résumés lower. So these reasonable views cannot simply become one answer.
